articles.title: Supreme Court to Consider Successive Habeas Claim in Capital Case, Twenty Years After the Murder
articles.content:
On Wednesday this week, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument in Guerrero, Director of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice v. Dexter Johnson. It is a capital case involving the kidnapping, rape, and murder of Maria Aparece that Johnson committed in 2006. The case does not involve any claim Johnson is innocent of these heinous crimes, but rather how to interpret provisions in the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA).
AEDPA prohibits successive habeas applications by state prisoners with only two narrow exceptions, including for claims that "rel[y] on a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable." 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(A). The question presented seems to answer itself. The Supreme Court has granted cert to decide whether a claim relies on a "new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable" when the Court announced the rule before the filing of the prisoner's prior federal habeas petition. As Texas persuasively argues in its merits brief, Johnson's Atkins claim (that he should not be executed because, he claims, he is borderline intellectually disabled) does not rely on any new rule of constitutional law. The Court decided Atkins v. Virginia in 2002—long before Johnson filed his initial federal habeas application, before his conviction became final on direct review—and even before he committed the capital murder for which he was sentenced to death.
Instead of a change in law, Johnson's claim relies on a new factual predicate: the publication of a new diagnostic manual by the American Psychiatric Association (the DSM-5), under which he was diagnosed with an intellectual disability. But a claim in a successive application based on a new factual predicate must satisfy § 2244(b)(2)(B), which Johnson's Atkins claim does not, because his new evidence has no bearing on whether the jury would have found him "guilty of the underlying offense." 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(B)(ii).
Surprisingly, a Fifth Circuit panel accepted Johnson's argument that he could pursue relief on this "new" claim. And the Fifth Circuit en banc denied further review by a vote of 9-7. Judge Ho (joined by Judges Jones, Smith, and Engelhardt) wrote a dissent from this denial, pointing out that "[e]xtraordinary delays like this are, alas, extraordinarily commonplace in our criminal justice system. And they are far from costless. Never mind the expense to the taxpayer. Such delays also force the family and friends of victims like Maria Aparece to wait for justice—for over two decades, in this case."
I have filed an amicus brief in the case, along with counsel of record Allyson Ho and her colleagues at Gibson Dunn, Brad Hubbard, Matt Scorcio, Brandon Wolf, and Marquan Robertson. Our brief provides a fuller account of the cost to victims' families—such as the Aparece family—who must wait for justice in capital cases like this one. Here's the introduction to our brief:
Twenty years ago, in the early-morning hours of Father's Day 2006, Dexter Johnson abducted 23-year-old Maria Chrisalee Lopez Aparece—"Sally" to her family and friends—and her boyfriend, Huy Ngo, at gunpoint. After terrorizing them, Johnson raped Sally in the back seat of her car while his accomplice taunted Ngo. Johnson then marched Sally and Ngo into the woods, shot each of them in the head, and left them for dead. Johnson and his accomplices then took Sally's car joyriding and used her credit cards to fund a shopping spree. Earlier that evening, Sally had been at home making a card for her father, Protasio Aparece, while he worked a sixteen-hour shift as a registered nurse. After her murder, Sally's family found the unfinished card. They placed it in their living room, in front of the fireplace, alongside Sally's ashes—where it remains today. Johnson's vicious crimes inflicted unbearable pain on his victims and their families.
But that was just the beginning of their suffering. Johnson's serial litigation has robbed the families of even a modicum of peace or closure. It has been two decades since Johnson brutally murdered Sally, and nineteen years since a Harris County jury sentenced him to death—but justice still has not been served. This Court should vindicate crime victims' "important interest in the timely enforcement of a sentence," Bucklew v. Precythe, 587 U.S. 119, 149 (2019), and "powerful and legitimate interest" in "real finality," Calderon v. Thompson, 523 U.S. 538, 556 (1998), by reversing the judgment below and ending an ordeal that has compounded the suffering of Sally's family for over two decades.
You can read the full brief for the Aparece family here, which discusses how excessive delays (like the one in this case) break AEDPA's promise of finality in capital cases and how research confirms that excessive delays in criminal cases harm victims' families.
I hope the Court reverses the Fifth Circuit's decision and brings the Aparece family one step closer to justice.
The post Supreme Court to Consider Successive Habeas Claim in Capital Case, Twenty Years After the Murder appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: State Governments Burden Residents With Growing Debt Just Like the Feds
articles.content:
California's state government, which has run up $11,511 in debt per resident, is asking voters to approve more billions of dollars in bonds, to be paid back by taxpayers at a later date. The cost of carrying that extra debt will be added to the roughly $6 billion the state pays each year to service bonds issued in the past. But the Golden State isn't the most debt-burdened state in the country. Connecticut and New Jersey are the most heavily burdened per capita, while Utah carries the least debt per person. The reasons for running up those obligations vary, but the heavier the load, the more taxpayers will have to carry in the years to come.
"Connecticut ($25,381 per capita) and New Jersey ($22,933) are the two state governments with more than $20,000 in debt per capita," according to this year's State and Local Government Finance Report from the Reason Foundation, which publishes Reason. "Hawaii ($19,553 per capita), Illinois ($17,859), Massachusetts ($17,536), and Delaware ($17,445) rank third through sixth in per-capita debt, each with more than $17,000 in debt per state resident."
"Utah, with $1,856 in per-capita debt, is the only state government in the nation with per-capita debt under $2,000," the report adds. Tennessee, South Dakota, Indiana, and Idaho also come in at under $3,000 in debt per state resident.
Overall, state governments around the U.S. reported $2.6 trillion in total debt and $1.9 trillion in long-term debt as of the end of fiscal year 2024. When local governments are added in, the total burden rises to $6 trillion in total debt and nearly $5 trillion in long-term debt.
"In per capita terms, New York ($37,006 per capita), New Jersey ($35,100), Connecticut ($33,189), Illinois ($31,582) and Hawaii ($30,759) have the highest total state and local debt, which includes debt at the state, county, city and school district levels within each state," notes the report.
At $6,228, Idaho has the lowest combined state and local per-capita debt burden, followed by Indiana, South Dakota, Tennessee, and West Virginia.
In terms of overall dollar owed, California has the most combined debt in the nation at $1.06 trillion in state and local debt. Given the large size of the state's population, that works out to $26,760 per resident, putting the state in eighth place.
There's nothing inherently wrong with debt when it's used to finance large one-off projects over time, like infrastructure, and when it doesn't rise to the level of an insurmountable burden on a state's taxpayers. But when it's used to pay for ongoing policies—such as affordable housing and immunology research, as addressed in California's 2026 bond proposals—that's a troubling indication that debt has become part of the regular funding process in a state and is likely to accumulate year after year.
California is among the states where very expensive political programs have consistently outstripped financial resources. Politicians have responded not by moderating their ambitions, but by borrowing money on an annual basis to pay for their wish lists.
"Both our office and the administration expect the state to face multiyear deficits, with estimates ranging from $20 billion to $35 billion annually," California's Legislative Analyst's Office warned in its overview of the governor's 2026-2027 budget. "After four years of projected deficits and a cumulative total of $125 billion in budget problems solved so far, the state's negative fiscal situation is now chronic…even as the state's economy and revenues have grown, underscoring that the problem is structural rather than cyclical."
While the scope of its problems is substantial, California is far from the only state to face rising debt burdens, often as the result of bad financial practices intended to satisfy short-term wants at the expense of long-term responsibility.
"The $5 trillion of long-term debt of state and local government consists of bonds, loans, and notes (42%), unfunded pension liabilities (32%), unfunded retiree health care (19%), accrued leave payouts/compensated absences (2%), and other (5%)," comments the Reason Foundation report. "The states with the highest per-capita long-term debt across their state and local governments are New Jersey ($32,794), Connecticut ($29,840), New York ($29,430), Illinois ($27,688), and Hawaii ($26,336)."
When it comes to public pension liabilities—a major source of pain for U.S. state governments and their taxpayers—Illinois is in the worst shape, with only 52 percent funding. At 104.2 percent funding, Tennessee is in the best condition. The median funding ratio for states is 78 percent, with state pension plans overall having $1.29 trillion in unfunded liabilities.
It's worth noting that the spendthrift habits of politicians are not new phenomena, and most states have tried to rein-in bad behavior by law or through their constitutions. All states but Vermont require at least some effort to balance budgets every year. But officeholders can be very creative in working around mandates that they spend no more than they collect.
Not to pick on California, but data on the state is widely available and some of its politicians' conduct is particularly egregious. In the Golden State, the courts have ruled that the budget complies with the state constitution if expenditures don't exceed estimated revenues.
"So, the Legislature sets forth its revenue estimate in the annual state budget bill and that estimate will essentially not be subject to review by a constitutional officer or a court," according to Capitol Weekly's Chris Micheli, an attorney. "The Legislature can adopt a 'balanced budget' based upon its determination that federal funds or new revenues are forthcoming, even though there is no guarantee of receipt of those funds."
It's easy to comply with balanced budget requirements while also spending more than you collect in taxes if you are free to make up numbers from thin air.
Again, borrowing and debt can be perfectly reasonable financial tools when used wisely to pay for big projects and unexpected emergencies. But for many states, as with the federal government, spending far more than can be afforded has become a matter of course.
The post State Governments Burden Residents With Growing Debt Just Like the Feds appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Can Milei's Success in Argentina Be Repeated Elsewhere?
articles.content:
The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.
In 1984, Milton and Rose Friedman published a short book called Tyranny of the Status Quo. President Ronald Reagan had been in office for more than three years, Margaret Thatcher had been prime minister for five, and the Friedmans were trying to explain a frustrating phenomenon: Politicians could win elections promising dramatic change, even arrive in office with a genuine mandate, and then discover that the existing machinery of government was unusually good at defending itself.
The Friedmans concluded that reformers had a narrow window of six to nine months to make big changes before bureaucracies adjusted, beneficiaries organized, legislators rediscovered their attachments to the old way of doing things, and the status quo reasserted itself. The obvious implication was that winning an election was not remotely the same thing as winning the day for small government and free markets.
In the United States, libertarians—to say nothing of the Libertarian Party—have had very little luck with even the first step of winning elections. Libertarian ideas have done considerably better than libertarian candidates, influencing tax policy, deregulation, criminal justice reform, school choice, and other areas without generally producing politicians eager to describe themselves as adherents of the whole package or finding voters excited to identify with the label.
A lifelong libertarian might be forgiven for getting a little pessimistic about the possibility of real reform.
Libertarians are accustomed to thinking of ourselves as intellectual insurgents and outsiders. We make arguments about what politicians should stop doing, and then complain when politicians inevitably keep doing those things. Argentine President Javier Milei's career raises a different prospect: What happens when someone who has spent years attacking the state—someone who has said "my contempt for the state is infinite"—is suddenly responsible for running it?
Milei wins elections while describing himself as an anarcho-capitalist. (While he regularly cites Milton and Rose, he may have more in common with their anarchist son David Friedman.) He won by taking to the airwaves to quote Friedman, Friedrich Hayek, Murray Rothbard, and other free market luminaries. He promised huge cuts, mass firings of government officials, and other radical changes.
In remarks at a September conference co-sponsored by Reason Foundation, the organization that publishes this magazine, Milei described his path from the "cultural battle" into electoral politics. For years, he said, he had been explaining the case for liberty. Then someone put a ballot in front of him and asked where those ideas appeared on it. "Ideas alone aren't enough," Milei concluded. If you want to change reality, you have to enter politics; once there, you have to produce results.
Milei moved quickly when first elected, perhaps mindful of the Friedmans' warning. National spending fell by roughly a quarter in real terms in his first year, and the government began posting surpluses within weeks. Exchange controls were loosened. From 25.5 percent in December 2023, monthly inflation first dipped below 2 percent in mid-2025; after rebounding slightly early this year, it fell to 1.7 percent in August. He cut 10 ministries, dissolved 29 public trust funds, and killed dozens of agencies. The privatization agenda has moved more slowly, in large part because of congressional resistance, but Milei's government has continued restructuring state enterprises and pushing them toward private ownership where it can.
Nearly three years into the Milei era, Argentina is not fixed. This issue of Reason takes a clear-eyed look at what has been accomplished, and what is yet to be done. Dollarization, central to Milei's initial campaign, has not happened; Nicolas Cachanosky argues that without a more durable monetary reform, Argentina remains vulnerable to a future reversal. Milei has behaved badly on press freedom, including using criminal complaints against journalists and supporting new restrictions that sit uneasily with his stated commitment to free expression. And yet most of Milei's impact has been a shocking triumph of libertarian ideals and ideas.
A libertarian in power was always going to encounter constraints that do not exist in books, essays, or panels. There was no doubt libertarian governance would suffer on contact with reality. But two years past the Friedmans' most optimistic estimate, the window of opportunity for real libertarian change remains open in Argentina.
Milei continues to set the agenda in his country, not merely to survive electoral challenges. His coalition won more than 40 percent of the vote in Argentina's October 2025 midterms, strengthening his position in Congress and giving him more room to continue his program. As Iván Carrino writes, Milei—perhaps following a playbook from his beloved Rothbard—may now have something libertarians have rarely possessed: the beginnings of a mass constituency for libertarian economic ideas.
The cover of this issue calls it "A New Argentina," borrowing the title of a song from Evita. The older political promise associated with that phrase in the Broadway musical was Peronist and expansive, built around a larger role for the state in Argentine life. The new version is considerably more peculiar and far more libertarian.
Reason's past coverage of Argentina supplies ample reasons for caution, and the Friedmans would remind us that the status quo may still come for Argentina in the end. But for this anarcho-capitalist libertarian, at least, Milei has provided a strong check on the pessimism that comes with being in the minority. He has shown that these ideas can move from books and think tanks onto a ballot, from a ballot into government, and from government into policy without immediately collapsing under the weight of political reality.
Can this experiment be repeated? The United States in 2026 is not Argentina in 2023. Libertarians elsewhere can't manufacture the kind of crisis Argentina was experiencing, and shouldn't want to. Argentina also has its own distinctive liberal tradition, including Jorge Luis Borges and Juan Bautista Alberdi. But Milei's presidency shows that when everything comes together and a window opens, a principled and committed politician can get a surprising amount done.

But Milei's presidency shows that when everything comes together and a window opens, a principled and committed politician can get a surprising amount done.

articles.title: Brickbat: Redeverbot
articles.content:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is again calling to end online anonymity, which he argues makes it difficult to identify those responsible for false information and personal attacks. Speaking at an event in Berlin, Merz was asked about whether informants and journalistic sources may sometimes need to remain anonymous. "Please, nobody come to me with free speech," Merz replied, without addressing the question. "This has nothing more to do with free speech," a concept he said was "at best" an American idea, "that I personally do not share." He compared the internet with newspapers, where publishers can be held accountable for what they print, and claimed that anonymous online messages make it harder to establish responsibility. He did later acknowledge that there may be legitimate reasons to allow anonymous speech but did not elaborate.
